subject: biology
title: Population genetics and the Hardy-Weinberg principle
key_idea: A population's gene pool is all its alleles, and allele frequency is how common each allele is. The Hardy-Weinberg principle predicts that frequencies stay constant if no evolutionary force acts. Selection, drift, the bottleneck effect and the founder effect change allele frequencies.

sections.heading: Populations, gene pools and allele frequency

blocks.text: Species exist as one or more populations. Populations are the units in which allele frequencies change.

items.meaning: A group of organisms of the same species, living in a particular place at a particular time, that can potentially interbreed.
All the alleles of all the genes in a population at a given time.
How often an allele occurs in the gene pool, as a proportion of all the alleles of that gene.

items: Allele frequency is the proportion of all the alleles of a gene that are one particular allele.
Evolution is a change in allele frequency in the gene pool.

blocks.text: The Hardy-Weinberg principle is a mathematical model. It predicts that allele frequencies will not change from generation to generation, so it can show when a population is changing.

items: The population is large, so chance has little effect.
Mating is random.
There is no selection: all genotypes survive and reproduce equally well.
There is no mutation.
There is no migration (no gene flow) into or out of the population.

blocks.label: Allele frequencies
where: p = frequency of the dominant allele
q = frequency of the recessive allele

blocks.label: Genotype frequencies
where: p² = frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype
q² = frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype

items.text: The only genotype you can see for certain is the homozygous recessive. Its frequency is q².
Take the square root of q².
This is the frequency of heterozygotes, the carriers.

blocks.text: Example: 4 in 100 people have a recessive condition, so q² = 0.04 and q = 0.2. Then p = 0.8 and 2pq = 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32.

diagram.alt: A Hardy-Weinberg practice question with new numbers each time: find the carrier frequency from the frequency of the recessive condition.
diagram.question: A recessive condition affects {a} people in every 10 000. Assuming the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, calculate the frequency of carriers (2pq) to 3 decimal places.
working: q² = {a} ÷ 10 000, so q is the square root of that value.

items: Start from q², the homozygous recessive, and work out q, then p, then 2pq.
The principle only holds when there is no selection, mutation or migration, mating is random and the population is large.
If allele frequencies change over generations, one of these conditions is not met.

sections.heading: Selection, genetic drift and the founder effect

blocks.text: Selection is not the only force that changes allele frequencies. Chance can also change them.

items: **Selection** changes allele frequencies when some genotypes survive and reproduce better. Stabilising selection keeps the mean, and directional selection moves the mean to one extreme.
**Genetic drift** is a random change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next, as some alleles are passed on by chance and others are not.
Drift matters only in small populations. In a large population, random events average out.
In a small population, an allele can be lost completely or become fixed (the only allele) by chance.

rows: A large population is cut to a few survivors by a disaster, such as disease or hunting.
The survivors carry only some of the alleles, so genetic diversity is low and frequencies differ from before.
A few individuals leave to start a new population in a new place.
The new population has only the alleles of its founders, so frequencies differ from the original population.

items: Genetic drift is a change in allele frequency by chance, important only in small populations.
Both the bottleneck effect and the founder effect reduce genetic diversity.
The new allele frequencies after either event are due to chance, not to the alleles being advantageous.

checks.q: State three conditions needed for the Hardy-Weinberg principle to apply.
checks.a: Any three from: a large population; random mating; no selection; no mutation; no migration.

checks.q: In a population, 1 in 2 500 babies is born with a recessive condition. Calculate the frequency of carriers.
Explain why genetic drift has a greater effect on allele frequencies in a small population than in a large one.
checks.a: In a small population, chance events change the proportion of alleles passed on by a larger amount, so an allele can be lost or become fixed. In a large population, random changes average out and have little effect on allele frequency.

items: Use the Hardy-Weinberg equation to see whether allele frequency is changing: calculate the frequencies in one generation, compare them with the next, and a difference shows that a factor such as selection is acting.
Reproductive isolation lets populations accumulate different genetic information over time, which can lead to new species (see Speciation).
You must be able to explain how selection, the founder effect and genetic drift, including the bottleneck effect, affect allele frequencies.
Both Hardy-Weinberg equations are provided in the exam, but you must state the conditions under which the principle applies.
Use the principle to calculate allele and genotype frequencies.
Factors that affect the evolution of a species: stabilising selection, directional selection, genetic drift, genetic bottleneck and the founder effect.
The equations p² + 2pq + q² = 1 and p + q = 1 are provided where needed, so you do not need to recall them.
